title: Diabetic Foot Ulcers
subject: Surgery
summary: Diabetic foot ulcers arise from neuropathy, ischemia and infection. Early recognition, staged assessment and multidisciplinary care are essential, especially where resources are limited.

sections.p: A non‑healing ulcer on the foot of a person with diabetes, usually with loss of protective sensation and/or vascular compromise.
b: Occurs in 15–25% of diabetics over 10 years
Often on plantar surface or pressure points

t.b: Loss indicates neuropathy, high ulcer risk

sections.p: The Wagner system classifies ulcers 0–5 based on depth and tissue involvement.
b: Grade 0: no ulcer, loss of sensation
Grade 3: deep to bone or abscess

sections.p: The triad of neuropathy, ischemia and infection drives ulcer formation.
Patients report painless sores, often with foul odour, swelling or drainage.
b: Callus formation or deformity increases pressure points

sections.p: Use simple, affordable tests to guide management.

t.b: Gram‑positive cocci or gram‑negative rods guide antibiotics

sections.p: Urgent referral needed for signs of systemic infection or impending gangrene.
b: Complications: osteomyelitis, Charcot foot, sepsis, amputation

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, provide wound care and monitor closely.
b: Educate patient on foot inspection and hygiene

exam: What is the first bedside test you would perform on a diabetic patient with a foot sore? — Monofilament to assess neuropathy, ABI for arterial disease.
How would you differentiate a neuropathic ulcer from a vascular ulcer? — Neuropathic: painless, callused, often plantar; vascular: dry, pale, with visible vessels.
A patient has a 2‑cm ulcer with purulent discharge. What antibiotic strategy is appropriate? — Broad‑spectrum covering gram‑positive and gram‑negative, adjust after culture.
The patient’s ABI is 0.6 but the ulcer is healing poorly. What is the next step? — Consider revascularisation or referral to vascular surgeon.
Why should NSAIDs be avoided in diabetic foot ulcer management? — They can worsen renal function and impair healing.
A diabetic foot ulcer shows no signs of infection but the patient has a fever. What is the likely complication? — Osteomyelitis or systemic infection; obtain X‑ray and blood cultures.
